# Suryagentic — Future Agentic Engineering ## SESSION 3 · Build Your First Working Agent ### Learner Lab Handout · 120-min Hands-On · No Coding Required --- ## 1. Goal Build an agent, entirely inside Claude, that reads a customer email, writes a calm reply, and sends it automatically — and escalates very-upset emails to a human instead of replying. --- ## 2. Before You Start - A Claude account (free tier is fine) - An email account you can connect to Claude - About 15 minutes of setup time --- ## 3. The Blueprint ``` TRIGGER BRAIN TOOLS OUTPUT ────────────────── ───────────────────────── ───────────────── ─────────────────────── Customer email → Claude + your instructions → Email connector → Reply sent to customer you paste in (or in the Project's Custom (reads & sends) — OR — Claude checks Instructions ESCALATE: human needed your inbox) Escalate-if-upset rule: very angry / refund / threats → stop, output ESCALATE, no auto-send ``` --- ## 4. Steps — Work Through Each Checkbox in Order **Step 0 — Create the Project** - [ ] In Claude, click **Projects** → **New Project** → name it **Order-Reply Assistant**. - *You should see:* a new Project page with a "Custom Instructions" panel on the left. **Step 1 — Paste the System Prompt** - [ ] Open Custom Instructions inside the Project and paste the full prompt from Section 5 below. Save. - *You should see:* the instructions appear in the panel; every chat you start here will use them automatically. **Step 2 — Add the Email Connector** - [ ] Inside the Project, click **Tools / Connectors** → add your email account → approve access when prompted (you can revoke this any time from your settings). - *You should see:* a green "connected" indicator next to the email connector. **Step 3 — Start a Chat and Paste the Customer Email** - [ ] Open a new chat inside the Project. Paste one of the test emails from Section 6 — or ask Claude: *"Check my inbox and show me the latest customer email."* - *You should see:* Claude acknowledge the email and confirm it has read the message. **Step 4 — Ask Claude to Handle It** - [ ] Type: **"Handle this email following my instructions."** Claude will draft the reply; with the email connector active it can also send. - *You should see:* either a drafted reply (warm, under 120 words) or the ESCALATE output — depending on which test email you used. **Step 5 — Confirm the Normal Reply** - [ ] Read the draft for the normal email. Check: name greeting, empathy line, promise of a 24-hour update, under 120 words, ends with "Warm regards, The Team." - *You should see:* all five criteria met before you approve sending. **Step 6 — Test the Escalation** - [ ] Paste the angry test email (Section 6) and repeat Step 4. The escalation rule is already baked into your instructions — no extra setup needed. - *You should see:* Claude output **ESCALATE: human needed** plus a one-line reason, and no reply sent. --- ## 5. COPY-THIS — System Prompt (paste verbatim into Custom Instructions) ``` You are the Order-Reply Assistant for our store. You read ONE incoming customer email and write a calm, warm, helpful reply. Rules: 1) Greet the customer by name if you can find it. 2) Acknowledge how they feel first, then address the issue. 3) For a late or missing order: apologize for the wait, say you're checking on it, and promise an update within 24 hours. 4) Keep it under 120 words, simple and friendly. Never argue. 5) If the customer seems very upset (insults, threats, ALL-CAPS anger, or asks to cancel or refund), do NOT reply automatically — output 'ESCALATE: human needed' and a one-line reason. Always end with: 'Warm regards, The Team.' ``` --- ## 6. Test Emails — Use These Exactly **Normal email (expect a calm reply):** > Hi, where is my order? It was due Monday. **Angry email (expect ESCALATE, no reply):** > This is RIDICULOUS! 5 days late. I want a REFUND. --- ## 7. Success Criteria | Test | What Claude must do | Pass? | |------|---------------------|-------| | Normal email | Greets customer by name (if available), expresses empathy, stays under 120 words, promises a 24-hour update, ends with "Warm regards, The Team." | ☐ | | Angry email | Outputs **ESCALATE: human needed** plus a one-line reason, does NOT auto-send any reply | ☐ | --- ## 8. If It Breaks | Symptom | Fix | |---------|-----| | No reply at all | Re-open the Project so the Custom Instructions load fresh, then try again | | Reply is odd or too long | Go back to Custom Instructions and tighten Rule 4 (e.g., add "maximum 100 words") | | Cannot send via the email connector | Check the connector's access under Settings → Connectors; re-approve if needed | | Escalating every email, even calm ones | Soften Rule 5 — remove one trigger condition (e.g., remove "ALL-CAPS") and save | --- *Suryagentic · Future Agentic Engineering · Session 3 of the Claude Mastery Series*

# Session 3 — Plain-English Glossary (every term, with examples) Whenever a term comes up in the session, here it is in plain words. --- ## AI Agent **What it is:** A software system that watches for something to happen, thinks about what to do, takes one or more actions using connected tools, and delivers a result — all without a human clicking through each step. **Everyday example:** You set it up once; after that, when a new customer inquiry lands in your email, the agent reads it, drafts a personalised reply, and sends it — while you are in a meeting. **SAP bridge:** Think of a background job in SAP that runs on a schedule and posts documents automatically — an agent does the same, but it can *reason* about what to do rather than just follow a fixed script. --- ## Chatbot (vs. Agent) **What it is:** A chatbot answers one question at a time and waits for your next message; an agent can carry out a multi-step task on its own, across many actions, without you prompting each step. **Everyday example:** A chatbot is like a vending machine — you press a button, it gives you one item. An agent is like a personal assistant who takes your one request and handles everything that follows. **SAP bridge:** A chatbot is like an SAP transaction screen where you fill in every field manually; an agent is like a workflow that fills, routes, and approves automatically once you kick it off. --- ## Trigger **What it is:** The event that starts an agent running — it tells the agent "now is the time to go to work." Nothing happens until the trigger fires. **Everyday example:** A new email arriving in your inbox is a trigger. The moment that email lands, the agent wakes up and begins. **SAP bridge:** In SAP, a workflow trigger is often a document status change (e.g., purchase order saved); an agent trigger works the same way — something happens, and work begins. --- ## Project **What it is:** In Claude, a Project is a dedicated workspace where you store the agent's Custom Instructions, its memory, and its connected tools — everything the agent needs lives in one place. **Everyday example:** Think of a Project as a labelled folder on your desk that contains the job description, the reference manuals, and the keys to the filing cabinet your assistant is allowed to use. **SAP bridge:** Similar to an SAP organisational unit or a business area — it defines the boundary and the rules for everything that happens inside it. --- ## Custom Instructions **What it is:** The written rules and background information you put inside a Claude Project that tell Claude who it is, what it should do, and how it should behave every single time it runs. **Everyday example:** It is like the employee handbook and job description you hand to a new hire on day one — Claude reads it before every conversation. **SAP bridge:** Comparable to configuration settings in an SAP role or a business-rules table: they define the boundaries and behaviour without anyone having to re-explain them each time. --- ## Large Language Model (LLM) **What it is:** A type of AI that has been trained on vast amounts of text and has learned to read, understand, summarise, and write language in a way that feels natural and human. **Everyday example:** Claude is an LLM. You type a question in plain English; Claude reads it, works out what you need, and writes back a clear answer — no special commands required. **SAP bridge:** Where SAP uses structured data and fixed logic to process information, an LLM processes *unstructured* language — emails, documents, free-text notes — and turns them into structured, actionable outputs. --- ## Model **What it is:** The specific version of an AI brain that does the thinking; different models have different capabilities, speeds, and costs. **Everyday example:** You might choose a faster model for simple sorting tasks and a more capable model for complex analysis — just as you might use a pocket calculator for addition but a spreadsheet for financial modelling. **SAP bridge:** Like choosing between SAP's standard reporting and SAP Analytics Cloud — same data, different processing power applied. > **For this course:** The model is always Claude. You will not need to choose or configure it — it is already selected inside your Project. --- ## Prompt **What it is:** The message or instruction you write to Claude that tells it what you want it to do right now. **Everyday example:** "Summarise this email in three bullet points and suggest a reply" is a prompt. The clearer and more specific the prompt, the better the result. **SAP bridge:** Like filling in the selection screen of an SAP report — the more precise your parameters, the more useful the output. --- ## System Prompt (= the Project's Custom Instructions) **What it is:** A special, behind-the-scenes prompt that runs *before* every conversation and sets Claude's role, rules, and knowledge — in a Claude Project, this is exactly what the Custom Instructions are. **Everyday example:** If you set the Custom Instructions to "You are a professional customer-service agent for a logistics company," Claude will respond in that role in every conversation, without you having to say it again. **SAP bridge:** Equivalent to default values and authorisation profiles that are applied automatically when a user logs into a specific SAP role — the setup is invisible to the end user but shapes everything they can do. > *System prompt* and *Custom Instructions* are the same thing in a Claude Project. You may hear both terms in the session — they refer to the same field. --- ## Context **What it is:** All the information Claude can "see" at any given moment — the Custom Instructions, the conversation so far, any documents you have pasted in, and the current message. **Everyday example:** If you paste in a five-page contract and then ask "What are the payment terms?", Claude uses the whole pasted document as context to find the answer. **SAP bridge:** Like the data available within a single SAP session — Claude can only work with what is currently in view; information outside the context window is not accessible. --- ## Connector **What it is:** A pre-built link between Claude and an external system (such as your email) that gives the agent the ability to read from or write to that system. **Everyday example:** The email connector lets Claude read incoming messages and send replies — you set it up once in the Project, and Claude can use it whenever the agent runs. **SAP bridge:** Similar to an RFC connection or an API integration in SAP — it is a configured bridge that lets two systems exchange data securely. --- ## Tool **What it is:** A specific capability that an agent can call upon to take action — for example, reading an email, searching a file, or sending a message. **Everyday example:** If an agent is a chef, tools are the utensils — a knife, a pan, a timer. The chef (Claude) decides which tool to pick up and when. **SAP bridge:** Like function modules or BAPIs in SAP — discrete, callable actions that the workflow engine can invoke at the right step in a process. --- ## Output **What it is:** The result that the agent produces at the end of its work — a written reply, a summary, a categorised list, or any other deliverable. **Everyday example:** After reading ten support emails, the agent's output might be a neatly formatted table: sender, issue type, suggested reply, and priority level. **SAP bridge:** Comparable to a processed document, a report, or an automatically posted entry in SAP — the tangible record that the work was done. --- ## Escalation / Human-in-the-Loop **What it is:** A designed pause in the agent's process where it stops and asks a human to review, approve, or decide before continuing. **Everyday example:** The agent drafts a refund response for a very large amount and then flags it: "This exceeds the standard limit — please review before I send." A human checks and approves; then the agent continues. **SAP bridge:** Exactly like a workflow approval step in SAP — the system holds the document and sends a work-item to a manager's inbox before processing can continue. --- ## Harness **What it is:** The overall structure — the Project, Custom Instructions, connectors, and escalation rules — that holds your agent together and makes it reliable and repeatable. **Everyday example:** A harness is like the scaffolding on a building site: it does not do the construction work itself, but it keeps everything in the right place so the work can happen safely and consistently. **SAP bridge:** Think of it as the combination of configuration, authorisations, and workflow definition in SAP — the invisible infrastructure that makes a business process run the same way every time. --- ## Token *(light touch)* **What it is:** The small chunks (roughly words or parts of words) that Claude breaks text into when reading and writing — tokens are how the model measures the size of text it processes. **Everyday example:** The sentence "Send the invoice" is about four tokens. Longer documents use more tokens, which affects speed and cost. --- ## What "Claude" Is *(light touch)* **What it is:** Claude is the AI assistant made by Anthropic — it is the LLM, the brain, and the conversational interface all in one product that you access through a browser or via a Project. **Everyday example:** When you open your Claude Project and start typing, you are talking directly to Claude. The agent you build in this session *is* Claude, configured with your Custom Instructions and connected to your email. --- ## Memory Aid — Three Lines to Take Home **The four parts of every agent:** > **Trigger** (something happens) · **Brain** (Claude thinks) · **Tools** (Claude acts) · **Output** (result is delivered) **The ladder of control:** > **Prompt** — shapes a single response · **Context** — shapes what Claude can see · **Harness** — shapes how the whole agent behaves, every time **The one-sentence summary:** > You write the rules once (Custom Instructions), connect one tool (your email), and Claude does the rest — that is your first working agent.
